body.p: Office Action Summary
Claims 17 and 31 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AlA), second paragraph, as being indefinite.

Claims 16-20 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian et al., (US20170097413A1) in view of Griesdorf et al., (US9989622B1) and in further view of Stivoric et al., (US20170156594A1).

Claim 21 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as modified by Griesdorf and Stivoric as applied to claim 18 above, and further in view of Hauenstein et al., (US20 170095181 Al), (hereinafter "Hauenstein").

Claim 24 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as modified by Griesdorf and Stivoric as applied to claim 16 above, and further in view of Alsheikh et al. (M. A. Alsheikh, S. Lin, D. Niyato and H. -P. Tan, "Machine Learning in Wireless Sensor Networks: Algorithms, Strategies, and Applications," in IEEE Communications Surveys & Tutorials, vol. 16, no. 4, pp. 1996-2018, Fourth quarter 2014, doi: 10.1 109/COMST.2014.2320099) and Simpson et al., (US20190336107A1).

Claim 25 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as modified by Griesdorf and Stivoric as applied to claim 20 above, and further in view Kim et al., "Tracking a Moving Target with Multipole Doppler Sensors Using an Artificial Neural Network", IEEE
Antennas and Propagation Society International Symposium, June 9-15, pp. 14771480, (hereinafter "Kim") and Rogers, (US20170351827A1) (hereinafter "Rogers").
Claim 26 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as modified by Griesdorf and Stivoric as applied to claim 17 above, and further in view of Sun and Komaromi.
Claims 27-30 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian in view of Griesdorf and Stivoric.
Claim 31 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as modified by Griesdorf and Stivoric as applied to claim 29 above, and further in view of Rogers.
Claim 32 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as modified by Griesdorf, Stivoric, and Rogers applied to claim 31 above, and further in view of Hlauenstein.

Claim 33 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as modified by Griesdorf, Stivoric, Rogers, and Hauenstein applied to claim 32 above, and further in view of DeLuca et al., (US6238338B1).
Claim 34 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as modified by Griesdorf, and Stivoric, applied to claim 27 above, and further in view Yuen et al., (US 20190186949 A1).
Claim 35 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian in view of Griesdorf and Stivoric.

Claim 22 was objected to as being dependent upon a rejected base claim, but would be allowable if rewritten in independent form including all of the limitations of the base claim and any intervening claims.
Claim 17 is amended to remove the term 'readily', and to recite that the health or fitness tracker application does not process the radio frequency based data. Claim 31 is amended

similarly. Support for this amendment is within the filed specification at page 4, lines 11-14 that describes (bolding added): "However, this RF based data may not be readily processed by health and fitness tracker applications having application programming interfaces (APIs) accustomed to operating with, for example, sensor data, such as x-y-z accelerometer data or other types of sensor data, indicative of the user's activity."
It is therefore respectfully submitted that claims 17 and 31 are now definite, and the Examiner is respectfully requested to withdraw the rejections based on Section 112.

The Examiner is respectfully requested to withdraw the rejections based on Section 103, because the prior art does not disclose or suggest the subject matter of the independent claims. MPEP 2143.03 (all claim limitations must be considered).

1. Independent claims 16, 27, 35: the prior art does not disclose or suggest wherein the pseudo sensor data is derived and provided to the second apparatus using the first apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker during a time interval when the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user that is associated with the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application is not provided, or when the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user is unavailable to the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application
Independent claim 16 has been amended to claim:
"wherein the pseudo sensor data is derived and provided to the second apparatus

using the first apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker during a time interval when the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user that is associated with the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application is not provided, or when the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user is unavailable to
the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application."
Independent claims 27 and 35 have been amended similarly.
Support for this amendment is found within the filed specification at least at page 3, lines 18-33, and page 4, line 38 to page 5, line 1.

Stivoric paragraph [0223] describes "Under such conditions, for example, if a sensor, for example an accelerometer, fails, the system might conclude that the wearer is sleeping or resting or that no motion is taking place. Under such conditions it is very hard to conclude if the data is bad or if the model that is predicting and making the conclusion is wrong. When an application involves both model and data uncertainties, it is very important to identify the relative magnitudes of the uncertainties associated with data and the model. An intelligent system would notice that the sensor seems to be producing erroneous data and would either switch to alternate algorithms or would, in some cases, be able to fill the gaps intelligently before making any predictions."

The Examiner stated on pages 5-6 of the Office Action, that Stivoric at the above- referenced excerpt ([0223]) describes a time interval when the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user is not provided or is unavailable. The Examiner also stated that Stivoric at the above-referenced excerpt ([0223]) describes a time interval when the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user is not provided or is unavailable, to reject claim 27 (Office Action, page 19) and claim 35 (Office Action, page 29).

However, the combination of the prior art including Stivoric does not disclose or suggest "wherein the pseudo sensor data is derived and provided to the second apparatus using the first apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker during a time interval when the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user that is associated with the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application is not provided, or when the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user is unavailable to the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application."

Stivoric paragraph [0223] at best describes "An intelligent system would notice that the sensor seems to be producing erroneous data and would either switch to alternate algorithms or would, in some cases, be able to fill the gaps intelligently before making any predictions."
However first, Stivoric also does not describe that such an intelligent system comprises a health or fitness tracker application.
Second, Stivoric does not describe a first apparatus providing pseudo sensor data to a

second apparatus when native sensor data is not provided, or when the second apparatus does not have access to native sensor data. Stivoric does not describe how to "fill the gaps intelligently". For example, Stivoric does not describe that when the sensor or accelerometer fails, a device associated with the sensor or accelerometer receives pseudo sensor data from another device.

Whereas in Applicant's case, when the user equipment 104 stops providing sensor data, the user equipment 104 receives the pseudo sensor data from the RF based tracker 110. Applicant's filed specification describes an implementation use case where a first apparatus (RF based tracker 110) derives pseudo sensor data from radio frequency based data using a machine learning model, and provides the pseudo sensor data to a second apparatus (e.g. a health and fitness tracker 104) during a time interval when the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user that is associated with the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker is not provided, or when the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user is unavailable to the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application.

This implementation use case is not described, disclosed, or suggested by the combination of the prior art including Gillian, Griesdorf, and Stivoric when considering Applicant's invention as a whole. When applying Section 103 to Applicant's claimed invention, the claimed invention should be considered as a whole per Hodosh v. Block Drug Co., Inc., 786 F.2d 1136, 1143 n.5 (Fed. Cir. 1986) ("when applying § 103: (1) the claimed invention must be considered as a whole").

Accordingly, the prior art does not disclose or suggest wherein the pseudo sensor data is derived and provided to the second apparatus using the first apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker during a time interval when the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user that is associated with the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application is not provided, or when the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user is unavailable to the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application. Independent claim 16, on the other hand, claims (with similar subject matter being recited in independent claims 27 and 35) "wherein the pseudo sensor data is derived and provided to the second apparatus using the first apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker during a time interval when the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user that is associated with the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application is not provided, or

when the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user is unavailable to the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application." This is not disclosed or suggested by the combination of the prior art. Therefore, independent claims 16, 27, and 35 are patentable and should be allowed.
Independent claim 16 has been amended to claim:
"providing, using the first apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker,

the pseudo sensor data derived from the radio frequency based data based on at least the machine learning model to a second apparatus comprising a health or fitness tracker application to enable the health or fitness tracker application to process the pseudo sensor data and native sensor data to enable tracking the activity and health or fitness of the user, wherein the first apparatus is different from the second apparatus, and the first apparatus is
configured to be separate from the second apparatus."
Independent claims 27 and 35 have been amended similarly.
Support for this amendment is found within the filed specification at least at page 3, lines 18-33.

Gillian paragraph [0077] describes "The user detection application 524 may detect, based on sensor data or radar data, presence of a user. In some cases, the user detection application 524 also tracks the user when the user is detected in the environment. For example, the user detection application 524 may detect the presence based on a detection radar feature 512 and shape radar feature 520 that matches a known 3D profile of the user. The user detection application 524 can also verify detection of the user through image data provided by the RGB sensor 220 or voice data provided by the acoustic sensors 212."

Gillian paragraph [0078] describes "In some embodiments, the activity detection application 526 uses the sensor data and the radar data to detect activity in the computing device 102's environment. The activity detection application 526 may monitor radar for detection features 512 and motion features 516. Alternately or additionally, the activity detection application 526 can use the acoustic sensors 212 to detect noise, and the RGB sensor 220 or depth sensor 224 to monitor movement."

Griesdorf Fig. 1A (corresponding to Fig. 1A of Griesdorf's priority application, namely US provisional application number 62/474,414 filed March 16, 2017, hereinafter "Griesdorf's provisional") shows a wireless communication device 102C, where the "wireless communication device 102C may receive the wireless signals transmitted by the wireless communication devices 102A, 102B." Refer to Griesdorf column 6, lines 12-15.

Griesdorf column 6, lines 6-55 (corresponding to paragraphs [0026]-[0027] of Griesdorf's provisional) describes in part "In the example shown, the wireless communication device 102C, operating in a state defined by modem parameters, processes the wireless signals from the wireless communication devices 102A, 102B and detects motion of an object in a space accessed by the wireless signals. For example, the wireless communication device 102C may perform the example process 400 of FIGS. 4A-4C, or another type of process for detecting motion."

The Examiner stated on page 4 of the Office Action, regarding claim 16, that Gillian at the above-referenced excerpts ([0077]-{0078]) describes "tracking the activity of the user." The Examiner applies the same rationale to reject the corresponding aspect of claim 27 (Office Action, page 18) and claim 35 (Office Action, page 27).

However, Gillian paragraph [0077] only describes detecting a user presence, and Gillian paragraph [0078] only describes detecting activity in an environment of a computing device and monitoring movement. Gillian does not describe a health or fitness tracker application.

The Examiner stated on page 5 of the Office Action, regarding claim 16, that Griesdorf at the above referenced excerpts (Fig. 1A, column 6, lines 6-55) describes the aspects related to a second apparatus comprising an application, where data is derived and provided to the second
apparatus, indicating that Griesdorf describes a device 102C that can process wireless signals sent by device 102A or 102B, and that those signals can be generated for motion detection.

However, Griesdorf at column 6, lines 6-55 only describes that device 102C detects motion (e.g., motion of an object in a space). Griesdorf does not describe that device 102C comprises a health or fitness tracker application.
Rogers Fig. 2 describes computing device 110.

Rogers paragraph [0031] describes "Computing device 110 includes or is able to communicate with a display 202 (six are shown in FIG. 2), a transceiver 204, one or more processors 206, and computer-readable storage media 208 (CRM 208). Transceiver 204 is capable of sending and receiving data directly or through a communication network, such as sensor data 108 from devices 106 through a local area, wide area, personal area, cellular, or near-field network."

Rogers paragraph [0032} describes "CRM 208 includes health manager 210, which includes or has access to sensor data 108, which may include sensor data 108 from one or multiple devices 106. This sensor data 108 can be associated with particular times 212 (e.g., respective time data), such that temporal proximity to patient situations 214 can be determined. Generally, patient situations 214 include an activity, emotion, environment, or physiological state. Activities include, for example, sleeping, walking, eating, working, exercising, driving, and talking."

Rogers paragraph [0037] describes "Each of noninvasive health-monitoring devices 106 may include a different health-monitoring sensor 306 having same or different modalities in which to measure a patient's health state or patient situation and other aspects."

The Examiner stated on page 15 of the Office Action, regarding claim 25, that Rogers at the above-referenced excerpts (Fig. 2, paragraphs [0031], [0032], [0037]) describes the aspect related to the application being a health and fitness tracker application. The Examiner applies the same rationale on page 22 of the Office Action to reject the aspect of claim 31 related to the
application being a health and fitness tracker application.

However, Rogers only describes computing device 110 receiving sensor data from the health monitoring devices 106 in order to determine a health state (implemented with health state 216 of computing device 110) of patient 102. The sensor data provided by the health monitoring devices 106 would correspond to the native sensor data claimed in claims 16, 27, and 35. Rogers does not disclose or suggest that the computing device 110 also processes pseudo sensor data, or that the health monitoring devices provide pseudo sensor data derived from radio frequency based data using a machine learning model.

Therefore, the combination of the prior art (Gillian, Griesdorf, and Rogers) does not disclose or suggest Applicant's claimed invention as a whole, including "providing, using the first apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker, the pseudo sensor data derived from the radio frequency based data based on at least the machine learning model to a second apparatus comprising a health or fitness tracker application to enable the health or fitness tracker application to process the pseudo sensor data and native sensor data to enable tracking the activity and health or fitness of the user" as claimed in claim 16 (with similar subject matter being recited in independent claims 27 and 35).

When applying Section 103 to Applicant's claimed invention, the claimed invention should be considered as a whole per Hodosh v. Block Drug Co., Inc., 786 F.2d 1136, 1143 n.5 (Fed. Cir. 1986) ("when applying § 103: (1) the claimed invention must be considered as a whole").

Accordingly, the prior art does not disclose or suggest providing, using the first apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker, the pseudo sensor data derived from the radio frequency based data based on at least the machine learning model to a second apparatus comprising a health or fitness tracker application to enable the health or fitness tracker application to process the pseudo sensor data and native sensor data to enable tracking the activity and health or fitness of the user, wherein the first apparatus is different from the second apparatus, and the first apparatus is configured to be separate from the second apparatus. Independent claim 16, on the other hand, claims (with similar subject matter being recited in independent claims 27 and 35) "providing, using the first apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker, the pseudo

sensor data derived from the radio frequency based data based on at least the machine learning model to a second apparatus comprising a health or fitness tracker application to enable the health or fitness tracker application to process the pseudo sensor data and native sensor data to enable tracking the activity and health or fitness of the user, wherein the first apparatus is different from the second apparatus, and the first apparatus is configured to be separate from the second apparatus." This is not disclosed or suggested in the prior art. Therefore, independent claims 16, 27, and 35 are patentable and should be allowed.
3. Even if it was obvious to combine the references, they do not disclose or suggest all of the elements/features of the claims, as explained above

Applicant respectfully traverses the rationale to combine the references to support a rejection under Section 103. For example, Stivoric does not describe that when the sensor or accelerometer fails, a device associated with the sensor or accelerometer receives pseudo sensor data from another device. Whereas in Applicant's case, when the user equipment 104 stops providing sensor data, the user equipment 104 receives the pseudo sensor data from the RF based tracker 110. Therefore, one skilled in the art would not be motivated to combine Gillian with Stivoric to arrive at Applicant's claimed invention. Further, because Griesdorf does not disclose or suggest a second apparatus comprising a health and fitness tracker application that processes pseudo sensor data, one skilled in the art would not be motivated to combine Gillian with Griesdorf to arrive at Applicant's claimed invention. Even if, for the sake of argument, it was obvious to combine the references, they do not disclose or suggest all of the elements/features of the claims as a whole, as explained above. When applying Section 103 to Applicant's claimed invention, the claimed invention should be considered as a whole per Hodosh v. Block Drug Co., Inc., 786 F.2d 1136, 1143 n.5 (Fed. Cir, 1986) ("when applying § 103: (1) the claimed invention must be considered as a whole").
4. Dependent claims

Though the dependent claims contain their own allowable subject matter, these claims should at least be allowable due to their dependence from allowable independent claims. Support for the amendment to claim 24 is within the filed specification at least at FIG. 2, FIG. 3A, and page 6, lines 26-30. To expedite prosecution at this time, no further comment will be made.
Conclusion

The Applicant respectfully requests the Examiner enter this amendment and pass the claims to issue. The undersigned representative welcomes the opportunity to resolve any matters that may remain, formal or otherwise, via teleconference at the Examiner's discretion.
Respectfully submitted,
